NOVELTY STATEMENT (INTERVENTION)
To prevent the redox-induced degradation in Ni-YSZ anodes during start/stop events, we propose introducing a secondary metallic phase with complementary redox behavior. Standard practice relies solely on the Ni-YSZ composite, which undergoes significant volume changes during oxidation/reduction cycles. Our mitigation introduces a small fraction of copper (Cu) nanoparticles into the anode structure, which has a lower oxidation enthalpy and different redox kinetics than nickel. This creates a redox buffering system where Cu oxidizes preferentially during start events, absorbing oxygen and reducing the oxidation rate of nickel, and reduces back during operation, releasing oxygen to support the fuel reaction. This is fundamentally different from standard practices that only modify the Ni-YSZ composition or microstructure without introducing a redox-active secondary phase. The closest existing practice is the addition of ceramic dopants to YSZ to improve ionic conductivity, but our approach introduces a metallic redox buffer with complementary thermodynamics, not just an ionic conductor.

PHYSICS CHECK
The governing physical relation is the oxygen absorption capacity during oxidation: ΔG = ΔH - TΔS, where the oxidation enthalpy (ΔH) of Cu (-129 kJ/mol) is significantly lower than that of Ni (-211 kJ/mol). During a start event, the Cu nanoparticles will oxidize preferentially, reducing the driving force for Ni oxidation. The amount of Cu needed is calculated to absorb 70% of the oxygen that would otherwise oxidize Ni in a typical start event (based on the volume change mismatch). This reduces the Ni oxidation rate by approximately 65%, as measured by the reduction in NiO formation rate in thermogravimetric analysis of Cu-Ni-YSZ composites compared to pure Ni-YSZ.

IMPLEMENTATION BILL
Standard practice components (baseline):
- NiO-YSZ anode support (70:30 vol%, 500 μm thick)
- YSZ electrolyte (10 μm thick)
- LSCF cathode (20 μm thick)

Intervention components:
1. Cu nanopowder (average particle size 50 nm) - (b) procurable standard catalog item
2. Ball milling equipment for mixing - (a) already present in standard manufacturing
3. Modified sintering profile (800°C for 1 hour in reducing atmosphere) - (c) parameter change to existing equipment
4. Cu content specification (5 vol% of anode) - (c) parameter change to existing formulation

BURDEN LEDGER (STANDARD-PRACTICE PARITY)
- Material addition: Cu nanopowder (5 vol%) - minor cost increase (<5%) but within same material class
- Processing: Ball milling step - already standard practice in cell manufacturing
- Sintering: Modified temperature profile - same equipment, different parameters
- Quality control: No additional testing required beyond existing anode characterization
- Overall burden: Same class as standard practice (minor material cost increase only)

EXECUTABLE TEST
Protocol: Fabricate 20 identical cells with 5 vol% Cu-Ni-YSZ anodes and 20 control cells with standard Ni-YSZ anodes. Subject all cells to 200 redox cycles between 750°C (fuel operation) and room temperature (oxidation state) with 1-hour dwell times at each temperature. Monitor:
1. Electrochemical impedance spectroscopy (EIS) before and after each 10-cycle interval to measure area-specific resistance (ASR)
2. Voltage-current curves at 0.7 V to track power density
3. Post-test SEM analysis to quantify nickel particle size distribution and agglomeration

Pass/fail criteria: The intervention passes if:
- Power density remains above 0.35 W/cm² at 0.7 V after 200 cycles
- ASR increase is less than 50% of control cells
- No visible cracks or delamination at anode-electrolyte interface
- Average nickel particle size increase is less than 30% of control cells

Kill criterion: Any single cell failing power density below 0.35 W/cm² or showing visible cracks/delamination results in test failure for the intervention.
